newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks plunge to 1-1/2 year low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia stocks plunge to 1-1/2 year low.

text.p: Malaysian stocks plunged to a 1-1/2 year low on Thursday on rampant selling triggered by foreign investors reacting to regional economic fears and better returns elsewhere, analysts said.
They said the market ignored strong supportive comments from the country's leaders and continued selling the big capitalised shares that pulled down the indices sharply.
The key Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index ended down 2.39 percent or 24.72 points at 1,008.52, after hitting a low of 1,002.36 a little while earlier.
On Wednesday, the Composite Index fell by 2.32 percent.
The market last closed below that level on January 2, 1996, when it ended at 993.18 points.
"There has been fierce program selling today," said the vice president of futures at a large local brokerage house.

The analysts blamed worries over rising domestic interest rates and possible ringgit volatility, which sparked shifting out of funds to other markets. They also cited spillover from the Thai baht crisis and the Cambodian clashes.
Analysts said the index looked weak technically and may fall further in coming days.

"(A rebound) is less likely to happen soon in Malaysia. It looks to me as though we're going down to about 960," John Schofield, regional technical analyst at Nava SC Securities in Hong Kong told Reuters Financial Television.
Bank Negara on Wednesday warned that it was willing to raise interest rates and even hinted at imposing capital controls to stamp out speculation in the ringgit.

Malaysian interbank bank rates surged across the board on Thursday, with the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) fixed at 8.38 percent in the morning, against 7.92 percent on Wednesday.
"When there are fears that the central bank will come out to implement capital controls, the market will react negatively," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities.
Verbal support of the market and the economy by both Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Tun Daim Zainuddin, economic adviser to the government, did not sway sentiment.
Anwar, also the Finance Minister, said there was no reason to undermine the ringgit due to the country's stability and its strong economic fundamentals.
Daim said stock prices are low enough to buy.
"The market is so low it is an opportunity to buy," he told reporters at a fund management conference. "It is a time for you to buy," Daim added.
"There has been no impact from Tun Daim (Zainuddin's) comments from this morning," a senior futures trader said.
Stockbrokers and fund managers said foreign funds were likely to continue trimming their Kuala Lumpur portfolios to take advantage of more attractive markets in the region.
"I think it's mainly because of divided attention in the region. A lot of foreigners are probably looking at Thailand, Indonesia," said Haizan Johari, investment manager at KL Mutual Fund.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
